XIII.1.title: Go first, work hard
XIII.1.reflection: Zilu asks about government: lead by example and work for the people. More? Do not tire. Book XIII, the book of government, begins with the shortest advice.
XIII.1.question: Where could you go first, before asking others?

XIII.2.title: Raise those you know
XIII.2.reflection: Zhonggong, steward to the Ji, asks about government: put officials to work, pardon small faults, raise the worthy. How can I know them all? Raise those you know; will others neglect those you do not? Good choices draw more good people in.
XIII.2.question: Whose small fault could you pardon this week?

XIII.3.title: Setting names right
XIII.3.reflection: Zilu asks what the Master would do first in Wei. Set names right. Zilu thinks it beside the point. If names are not right, speech does not accord with things; then affairs fail, ritual and music decline, punishments miss their mark, and the people do not know where to put hand or foot. The junzi's words must be things he can act on. In Wei at that moment, a son and a father were fighting over the throne, so the names were literally in dispute.
XIII.3.question: What word in your life no longer matches what it names?
XIII.3.exercise: Find one word you used today carelessly, and say plainly what you meant.

XIII.4.title: An old farmer knows better
XIII.4.reflection: Fan Chi asks to learn farming and gardening. Ask an old farmer, an old gardener. When he leaves, Confucius calls him a small man: if those above love ritual, rightness and good faith, people will come from all sides with their children on their backs; what need of farming? The chapter shows Confucius's view of his role and the limits of his world, which divided those who govern from those who farm.
XIII.4.question: What knowledge do you dismiss as beneath your role?

XIII.5.title: Three hundred odes and no use
XIII.5.reflection: Someone who can recite the three hundred Odes but cannot carry out a government task or answer on his own as an envoy: what use is all that learning? Knowledge must be usable.
XIII.5.question: What do you know by heart that you have never used?

XIII.6.title: Orders without example
XIII.6.reflection: If the ruler is upright, things get done without orders; if he is not, orders are not followed. The force of example, once more, against the force of command.
XIII.6.question: What do you order that you do not do?

XIII.7.title: Brothers in decline
XIII.7.reflection: The governments of Lu and Wei are brothers. Their founders were brothers, and now their disorder is alike. A one-line political joke.
XIII.7.question: Which two institutions you know have declined in the same way?

XIII.8.title: Good enough
XIII.8.reflection: Jing, a prince of Wei, lived well within his means: with a little he said it was quite enough; with more, quite complete; when rich, quite splendid. Contentment at each stage, rather than wanting the next.
XIII.8.question: At what stage would you say "this is enough"?

XIII.9.title: Many, rich, taught
XIII.9.reflection: Arriving in Wei, Confucius exclaims at the crowds. What more? Make them prosperous. And then? Teach them. The order is plain: people first, livelihood second, education third.
XIII.9.question: In a place you care about, which of the three comes first now?

XIII.10.title: Within a year
XIII.10.reflection: If a ruler would employ me, in a year things would be acceptable and in three years done. A rare boast, from a man long out of office.
XIII.10.question: What could you set right in a year, if you were given the means?

XIII.11.title: A hundred years of good men
XIII.11.reflection: If good men governed a state for a hundred years, they could overcome cruelty and do away with killing. Confucius quotes the saying and agrees. Reform is slow, measured in generations.
XIII.11.question: What change do you hope for that would take longer than your life?

XIII.12.title: A generation
XIII.12.reflection: Even if a true king arose, it would take a generation for ren to prevail. Another measure of patience.
XIII.12.question: What good thing are you expecting to happen too quickly?

XIII.13.title: Correct yourself first
XIII.13.reflection: If one corrects oneself, what difficulty is there in governing? If one cannot correct oneself, how correct others? The same thought as XII.17, said to everyone who would govern.
XIII.13.question: Whom are you trying to correct whose fault you share?

XIII.14.title: Family affairs
XIII.14.reflection: Ran Qiu comes late from court and says there was government business. Confucius: you mean the family's affairs. If it were government business, I would have heard of it, though I am not in office. He refuses to call the Ji family's private council by the name of government.
XIII.14.question: What private business is passed off as public around you?

XIII.15.title: One saying to raise or ruin a state
XIII.15.reflection: Duke Ding asks if one saying can make a state flourish. Not quite, but: it is hard to be a ruler. If a ruler knows that, it is nearly so. And one that can ruin it? The saying "my only joy in ruling is that no one contradicts me". If his words are good, fine; if not, and no one objects, that is nearly ruin.
XIII.15.question: Who is allowed to contradict you?

XIII.16.title: Near and far
XIII.16.reflection: The Duke of She asks about government: make those near happy, and those far will come. Good government is visible from outside.
XIII.16.question: What would make those near you glad?

XIII.17.title: Not in haste
XIII.17.reflection: Zixia, governor of Jufu, asks about government. Do not seek speed; do not look to small gains. Haste prevents thoroughness, small gains prevent great things.
XIII.17.question: What are you rushing that needs to be done thoroughly?

XIII.18.title: The father who stole a sheep
XIII.18.reflection: The Duke of She boasts that in his land the upright son testifies when his father steals a sheep. Confucius answers that where he comes from, the father covers for the son and the son for the father, and uprightness lies in that. It is one of the hardest chapters for a modern reader, because it puts family loyalty above public justice. It states the view of its time plainly, and the book does not hide it.
XIII.18.question: Where do you draw the line between loyalty to your own and honesty to everyone?

XIII.19.title: Even among the tribes
XIII.19.reflection: Fan Chi asks about ren. Be respectful at home, serious in work, loyal with others. Even among the barbarians, these may not be set aside. Goodness travels.
XIII.19.question: Which of the three would you keep in a place where no one expected it?

XIII.20.title: Grades of the shi
XIII.20.reflection: Zigong asks what makes a shi, an officer or scholar. Shame in one's own conduct and not disgracing one's ruler abroad. Next below: filial at home, brotherly in the village. Below that: true to one's word and resolute in action, stubborn little people, still the next grade. And today's officials? Mere measures of grain, not worth counting.
XIII.20.question: In your own scale of people, what comes first?

XIII.21.title: The ardent and the cautious
XIII.21.reflection: If I cannot find people who walk the middle way, I will take the ardent and the cautious. The ardent go forward; the cautious refrain from some things. Both extremes are preferred to having no drive at all.
XIII.21.question: Are you more ardent or more cautious, and how does it serve you?

XIII.22.title: Without constancy
XIII.22.reflection: A southern saying: a person without constancy cannot even be a shaman or a healer. Good! Then a line: one who is not constant in virtue will meet disgrace, and Confucius adds that this comes simply from not attending to the oracle. The chapter does not name its source, but the line is the Book of Changes, hexagram 32, Constancy: the one place the Analects quote it.
XIII.22.question: In what part of your life are you least constant?

XIII.23.title: Harmony without sameness
XIII.23.reflection: The junzi seeks harmony but not sameness; the small man seeks sameness but not harmony. Legge's "affable, not adulatory" is one reading. The more common one is about agreement: one can live in harmony with others without echoing them.
XIII.23.question: Where do you agree just to keep the peace?

XIII.24.title: Liked by everyone
XIII.24.reflection: Someone liked by everyone in the village: not yet enough. Disliked by everyone: not enough either. Better that the good in the village like him and the bad dislike him. Popularity is no test.
XIII.24.question: Whose dislike of you would you take as a compliment?

XIII.25.title: Easy to serve, hard to please
XIII.25.reflection: The junzi is easy to serve and hard to please: you cannot please him by wrong means, and he uses people according to their capacities. The small man is hard to serve and easy to please, and expects everything of everyone.
XIII.25.question: Are you easy to serve, for those who work with you?

XIII.26.title: Ease without pride
XIII.26.reflection: The junzi is at ease but not arrogant; the small man is arrogant but not at ease. Pride, the chapter suggests, is a form of unease.
XIII.26.question: When were you proud because you were not at ease?

XIII.27.title: Near to ren
XIII.27.reflection: Firm, resolute, simple and slow of speech: these are close to ren. Four plain qualities, none of them clever.
XIII.27.question: Which of these four do you have?

XIII.28.title: Among friends and brothers
XIII.28.reflection: Zilu asks what makes a shi. Earnest in urging and kind in manner: earnest among friends, kind among brothers. The bold disciple is told to soften at home.
XIII.28.question: Do you treat friends and family with the same tone, and should you?

XIII.29.title: Seven years of teaching
XIII.29.reflection: When a good man has taught the people for seven years, they can be sent to war. Even soldiers must first be taught.
XIII.29.question: What would you need years of preparation for before you could face it?

XIII.30.title: Throwing them away
XIII.30.reflection: To send untaught people to war is to throw them away. The book of government ends with a sentence against wasting lives.
XIII.30.question: Where are people being sent unprepared into something hard?
